title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to test whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair, one allowed repair) materially increases verifier-level semantic correctness for natural-language → low-level network-configuration translation. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. For each intent a single initial model generation was shared across baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call if the verifier failed that initial candidate. Results (confirmatory): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%), guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.0066667 (0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations = 0 (IQR = 0). Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow yielded a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over an already near-ceiling baseline. We bound this empirical outcome to the provided synthetic corpus, single model, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, and deterministic validator and highlight the methodological lesson that pilot baseline calibration is necessary to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces aim to reduce NetOps friction by translating human operator intents into concrete low-level configuration sequences for execution or review. Prior work shows that large language models (LLMs) can produce useful configuration templates but often make syntactic errors, omit required actions, or produce unsafe sequences that necessitate downstream correction [1]. Deterministic verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines are a common defensive architecture intended to detect and, if possible, automatically correct such errors before execution [2], [3]. Separately, security analyses show that textual claims can be converted into harmful tool calls in agentic LLM pipelines, motivating runtime gating and auditable decision points [4], [5].

Research question. Motivated by these operational concerns, we preregistered and executed the confirmatory question: Does constrained prompting (structured templates + semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? We froze the design, analysis plan, and execution contract before observing any model outputs (preregistration id: study_cand_2026_b2_v1). The design deliberately measured the deterministic validator pass/fail as the primary, machine-checkable endpoint to map generative outputs to a verifiable safety/correctness predicate.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial, artifactized end-to-end, that operationalizes verifier pass/fail as the primary endpoint for NL→configuration translation. (2) A complete execution and analysis archive (N=150 paired items; completed episodes = 300; model calls used = 151) comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus at most one verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. (3) An artifact-grounded empirical finding: on the supplied synthetic corpus the guarded pipeline produced a negligible numerical improvement (0.67 percentage points) over an already near-ceiling baseline; we draw the methodological implication that pilot baseline calibration is necessary in preregistered NetOps trials to avoid ceiling effects that undermine power assumptions.
sections.related_work:
This study sits at the intersection of three recent streams. First, prior intent-to-configuration work documents the challenge of mapping free-text operator intents to verifier-sound artifacts and reports modest semantic-correctness rates on public benchmarks [1]. Second, generate→verify→repair approaches—ranging from verifier-aware fine-tuning to policy-guided iterative repair—often report improved correctness when deterministic or policy-guided verifiers are used as oracles for repair [2], [6]. Third, attack and defense analyses for agentic LLM pipelines highlight claim-to-action vulnerabilities and motivate runtime mitigations such as prompt-hardening, tool-call gating, and verifier-aware planning [4], [5].

Where our trial differs: (a) we used shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (one initial sampled candidate shared across conditions), (b) we bounded repair to at most one additional model call per intent, (c) evaluation used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and (d) the task bank is synthetic and constrained to verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes). These precise design choices affect how numerical outcomes should be interpreted relative to prior work that used different sampling semantics, repair budgets, or model sets.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration, design and estimands. The trial pre-registered study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and froze the confirmatory estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The primary test is an exact two-sided McNemar test on paired pass/fail outcomes with bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration (SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399) and the execution contract are archived in the artifact bundle.

Generation semantics and shared_initial_candidate interpretation. The execution adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial model generation was produced per intent and that same sampled initial candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call only when the deterministic verifier failed that initial candidate. Consequently, the observed baseline success rate measures the validity of the single initial sampled candidate; the guarded vs baseline contrast therefore isolates the marginal effect of the single allowed repair applied to the identical initial sample. This semantics is important for precise causal interpretation and is recorded in deterministic_reconciliation.json and the execution manifest.

Task bank, inclusion/exclusion, and synthetic corpus. Confirmatory sample: N=150 distinct synthetic intents generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 covering four intent families (reachability/isolation, ACL-like, VLAN/MTU sequence changes, uplink switchover patterns). Topologies were restricted to verifier-capable small networks (4–32 nodes). A rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/verifier-coverage unit-tests were applied deterministically prior to model calls; no confirmatory exclusions occurred (exclusions = 0). Task seeds, reference answers, required sequences, and expected final states are archived for every task in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Model, validator, and runtime sampling. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) implementing a full-intent-constraint validation rule that returns a boolean pass/fail plus a normalized configuration text. Reviewer-requested clarification (explicit and artifact-grounded): execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). The run did not enforce a deterministic sampling temperature or fixed random seed for the LLM; therefore model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent API sessions. All per-call runtime sampling metadata and provider-call logs are archived in execution/provider_calls and execution/responses artifacts for independent inspection.

Adapter constraints, repair budget, and call accounting. Adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 enforced a budget of one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call per intent (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). The run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 300) and used 151 model calls in total (model_calls_used = 151). The adapter's per-stage call counts are recorded in deterministic_reconciliation.json (shared_initial_generation = 150; repair = 1). Each model call executed in a fresh isolated API session per the preregistered contamination checks.

Scoring, primary analysis and missingness treatment. The deterministic validator's boolean verdict defined semantic correctness (primary binary endpoint). Primary analysis used an exact McNemar two-sided test on the paired contingency table (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00) and computed bootstrap percentile 95% CI from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistered missingness plan used complete-pair analysis; there were no missing or unscorable episodes in this run. All analysis code and intermediate CSV summaries (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv) are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. Planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1; exclusions = 0; contamination flags = 0. The analysis/missingness_summary.csv confirms zero missing or unscorable episodes.

Primary numerical outcomes. The paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline) were: n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (~0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These numbers are reported verbatim from analysis/results.json and analysis artifacts.

Repair diagnostics and revision counts. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150), consistent with the near-ceiling initial success rate. Median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). The single repair converted one initially invalid candidate to a valid configuration under the deterministic validator; validator traces for that task record repair_applied = true and the repair prompt/response artifacts are present in execution/provider_calls for inspection.

Representative artifact-grounded examples. Representative tasks in the execution bundle illustrate typical intents and validator traces. For task-000001 the intent required shutting edge1 down, updating MTU and VLAN, then restoring admin up. The shared initial, baseline, and guarded responses all matched the reference four-command sequence; validator_trace.validation_after shows parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, normalized_configuration equal to the reference, and valid = true. Similar artifact-backed examples for tasks 000002–000006 are included in the execution manifest and exemplify a range of difficulty patterns ("make_before_break_uplink_switchover", paired_link_atomic_mtu_change, rolling_access_vlan_migration) with observed validity counts as summarized in analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Statistical interpretation. The preregistered power analysis targeted detecting an absolute increase of ~15 percentage points with N=150 under conservative discordant assumptions; the observed baseline (149/150) produced a ceiling effect that invalidated those assumptions. The observed contingency (n_10=1, n_01=0) yields an exact McNemar p = 1.0 and a narrow bootstrap CI near zero; the data therefore provide no evidence of a meaningful guarded improvement under the registered semantics and repair budget on this corpus.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and implications for preregistration. The core methodological lesson is that preregistered confirmatory LLM-for-NetOps trials must include a short pilot to estimate baseline initial-candidate correctness with the chosen model and prompts prior to fixing sample size. Here the pilot assumption (baseline substantially below ceiling) did not hold, and the resulting near-ceiling baseline reduced the ability to detect the preregistered target effect.

Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because we used shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded pipeline could only change outcomes by applying the single allowed repair to the identical initial sample. Thus our estimand measures the marginal benefit of at most one repair applied to the same initial generation. Alternative semantics—independent per-condition sampling, multiple repair iterations, or larger repair budgets—could yield different empirical contrasts and should be the focus of future confirmatory designs.

Operational value beyond binary verifier pass/fail. Even when numerical improvements are negligible under a single binary endpoint, guarded pipelines provide important operational artifacts: auditable verifier verdicts, explicit repair prompts suitable for operator dashboards, and enforced gating points for human approval. These non-statistical operational benefits are not captured by the single binary endpoint but are documented in the execution artifacts (validator verdicts, normalized configurations, and repair prompts).

Relation to prior work. Our artifact-grounded outcome does not contradict prior demonstrations of larger repair benefits; prior studies often evaluate lower baseline competence, independent sampling semantics, or multi-iteration repair channels. We provide a narrowly bounded empirical measurement of a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator.

Threats to validity. Internal: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate marginal repair but do not capture inter-condition sampling variance. Construct: the deterministic validator's pass/fail is only as good as the mapping and verifier coverage; we executed preregistered unit-tests for mapping code prior to model calls to reduce this threat (unit-test results are archived). External: single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic tasks, and small topologies (4–32 nodes) limit generalization to production WANs and vendor-specific CLIs. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation was invalidated by the ceiling baseline; inferential claims about larger effects are therefore unsupported in this dataset.

Practical recommendations. We recommend (1) a short pilot to estimate baseline competence before locking sample size; (2) explicit specification of generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) to match the estimand; (3) preregistered repair-budget sensitivity analyses (one vs multiple repairs); and (4) automated validator-coverage tests and mapping unit-tests run and archived prior to model calls to detect mis-evaluations early.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting with constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the archived synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific takeaway is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials should include pilot baseline calibration so that task difficulty and sample size preserve statistical power and avoid ceiling effects. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
